<reason>Side B won the decisive clashes. B's dilemma about fee size (too small to change behavior vs. too large and punitive) was never fully resolved by A, who pivoted to "cost recovery alone justifies it" [A4.1] — a shift B sharply exposed as abandoning the opening's safety rationale. B answered both pressure questions directly and coherently (tolls track use and harm; price the space itself), while A's "they never answered" in Rebuttal 2 was premature, that speech was clipped before completion, and A misreferenced nonexistent IDs [C2.6, C2.3]. A also misdescribed liability insurance [A2.3], which B corrected effectively. A's strongest material — the AEB-doesn't-change-physics point [A2.2], the curb-footprint pressure, and the "size is the cost" reframe — kept the debate close, but B's closing delivered an unanswered final blow: even granting that size is the cost, the motion charges a categorical tier, not a per-foot or per-pound scale, so on A's own theory the instrument fails to track the harm. B's consistent "price use, not shape" through-line and memorable phrasing made the choice easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1–B4.2: B directly answered A's "pure tax" pressure question by distinguishing cost-recovery tools that scale with use from a static size surcharge, then turned A's own "cost recovery alone justifies it" retreat into evidence that the safety justification had been abandoned — reinforced by the closing trap that the motion enacts a cliff while PRO defended a sliding scale.</best_rebuttal>
